prohibited_recommendations: Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
Do not use neuromuscular blockade outside intubation context.
required_recommendations: Intubate and mechanically ventilate; ICU admission.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

key_clinical_evidence: Severe AIDP with respiratory failure mandates ICU and ventilation.
Post-Campylobacter cases warrant repeat EMG for AIDP-vs-AMAN clarification at 1–2 weeks.
Autonomic instability is a leading cause of mortality in severe GBS — continuous monitoring is mandatory.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: Five-day rapidly progressive ascending leg weakness and areflexia with bilateral facial diplegia, preceded by Campylobacter gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago. Unable to walk. Respiratory function declining.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 35-year-old physical therapist presenting with a 5-day history of rapidly progressive neurological symptoms. Two weeks before admission, he had confirmed Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis (stool culture positive at an urgent care clinic) lasting 4 days. He recovered but 10 days later developed bilateral foot tingling. Over the following 5 days, weakness ascended rapidly from his feet to his hips. He is now unable to walk. Yesterday he noticed bilateral facial drooping and slurred speech. He has had dysphagia for thin liquids since this morning. As a physical therapist, he recognized the pattern immediately and came to the ED. FVC on arrival is 1.8 L (43% predicted). He is alarmed and asking for IVIG. He has no bowel or bladder symptoms. No neck stiffness. No fever since his gastroenteritis resolved.

neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 1.8 L (predicted 4.2 L — 43% predicted; 22 mL/kg). NIF: -24 cmH2O — AT INTUBATION THRESHOLD.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral mild facial diplegia — both upper and lower face involved, forehead included. Mild dysarthria. Gag intact. No diplopia.
neurological_exam.gait: UNABLE TO WALK. Unable to stand without bilateral support.
neurological_exam.motor: Severe bilateral lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 2/5, knee extension 3/5, ankle dorsiflexion 2/5. Upper extremity: shoulder abduction 3+/5, elbow flexion 4/5, grip 4/5. Cannot rise from chair without arm support.
neurological_exam.reflexes: GLOBAL AREFLEXIA — absent bilaterally at all tendon reflexes including bilateral biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, Achilles.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral distal glove-and-stocking paresthesias and numbness. Vibration absent at bilateral ankles and reduced at bilateral wrists.
